sections.title: Recognizing the species
sections.text: Lactarius picinus is a sturdy milkcap with a very dark brown to blackish cap, matte and finely velvety. The centre may become slightly depressed with age. The fairly crowded gills are whitish to cream. The cylindrical stem is brown to grey-brown, sometimes paler beneath the cap and towards the base; it often becomes hollow at maturity.

sections.title: Cut surface and useful characters
sections.text: The whitish flesh may turn pink to orange after cutting. The milk is white and does not change colour when observed by itself; in contact with the flesh it may turn pink. Both the milk and flesh taste acrid. The spore print is ochre. Consider these characters together: none alone guarantees an identification.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: This ectomycorrhizal species grows on soil in damp conifer forests, especially with spruce; fir is also reported as a possible host. It is recorded from late summer into autumn, generally from August to October.

sections.title: Lookalikes and safety
sections.text: Lactarius lignyotus can look similar, but is usually smaller and has more strongly decurrent gills; Lactarius fuliginosus is more often associated with broad-leaved trees. Taxonomic treatments differ: some references retain L. picinus as a species, while the French ADONIF catalogue includes it within L. fuliginosus. The Czech Myko Atlas lists it as inedible; this reference entry does not recommend consumption.

traits: Very dark brown to blackish cap, matte and finely velvety, often slightly depressed in the centre when mature
Fairly crowded, whitish to cream gills
Cylindrical brown to grey-brown stem, paler beneath the cap or towards the base, often hollow at maturity
Whitish flesh turning pink to orange after cutting; white milk unchanged by itself, sometimes pink where it meets the flesh, with an acrid taste
Damp conifer forests, especially with spruce · late summer and autumn
Taxonomic treatments differ: retained as a species by some sources, included in Lactarius fuliginosus by the French ADONIF catalogue
safetyNote: Taxonomic and ecological reference only. One mycological source lists it as inedible; do not eat a mushroom identified from this entry.
